Australian Article On "Marijuana Addicts" Illustrates How Prohibitionism
Can Interfere With Treatment of People Who Are Truly Cannabis Dependent

Consequently, people who are truly having problems with cannabis dependence may have difficulty getting competent treatment.

Bad journalism, as usual, plays a role in sustaining the confusion that makes it more difficult for people to get competent help and for people of good will to know how to provide it.

Sadly, this program is being sponsored by the Anglican Church.)

LIVE IN COURSE TARGETS MARIJUANA ADDICTS
From The Advertiser
http://www.advertiser.com.au/
advedit@ozemail.com.au

January 28, 1999
By Barry Hailstone and Melissa King

AUSTRALIA’S first treatment program for cannabis users who want to quit has begun at Port Adelaide.

The Archway Rehabilitation and Community Service will provide eight-week residential and outpatient course for about 120 people a year.

The program was modelled on those run by the Betty Ford Clinic is the United States and the US armed forces’ program for treatment of drug addiction, the coordinator, Mr Nick Gill, said yesterday.

The courses, the first of their kind in Australia, will target the 10 per cent of cannabis users who become dependent on the drug.

(Marijuananews note: This number is stated as though it were an established fact, but it is definitely not. Consider that in order to know a percentage one must first know the whole. How many cannabis users are there? Under marijuana prohibition it is extremely difficult to know this. The Dutch recently lowered their estimates of the number of Dutch cannabis users by almost half.

Also, it is like that the percentage of users who have problems will be greater under prohibition than would otherwise be the case, because use will be most prevalent in the most abuse prone segment of the population. The Dutch have outpatient programs for "cannabis addicts" -- their English translation of their Dutch term. Around one percent of regular users seek help.

See

This is roughly twice the earlier estimate that three to five per thousand users have problems, because – as noted – they only have half as many regular users as thought.

See

Very simply, some users are self-medicating and their "dependence" may actually be beneficial. For example, people who are "Prozac-dependent" may be described as just following doctor’s orders by taking a drug which helps them.)

Mr Gill said alcoholics with a secondary dependence on cannabis would also be treated.

"It has been shown that 36 per cent of (cannabis) users say they are unable to stop drinking once they start," he said.

(Marijuananews note: This is utter non-sense. This would mean that 36% of cannabis users are alcoholics. There is simply no data to support this. There may be a higher rate of marijuana use among alcoholics than among the general population, but that would say nothing about cannabis use or abuse per se. They would be alcoholics -- even if cannabis did not exist.)

"Thirty-four per cent of those had caused or received injury as a result of their drinking."

Mr Gill said 9 percent of alcohol-cannabis dependent dependent users said they "needed a morning drink to function".

(Marijuananews note: I may need a drink after I finish this.)

"Cannabis is as addictive as alcohol for people who have a disposition to addiction," he said.

Alcohol withdrawal can be fatal. Cannabis withdrawal, if it exists, is very mild. It is necessary to inject a synthetic cannabis-receptor blocker into mice in order to get them to show withdrawal symptoms. Even then, they are much less severe than alcohol withdrawal.)

"For every person who is dependent, they have a significant, disruptive effect on the lives of at least 10 other people."

Cannabis addicts usually smoked every day, and suffered decreased short-term memory, low attention span, and difficulty with learning and complex tasks.

(Marijuananews note: This is from a study of marijuana smokers published in the Journal of the American Medical Association.

Those suffering from "full-blown cannabis psychosis" - usually long-term users who took large concentrations of the drug - were likely to become incoherent and violent, and risked a greater predisposition towards schizophrenia.

(Marijuananews note: Now we are into full-blown reefer madness. There is nothing to support this.)

People seeking admission to the program would be screened for cannabis dependency and be required to submit urine samples for analysis.

Those with the most severe dependency would be offered a place in the residential program, while other would undertake an outpatient program.

Mr Gill said the first residential program had begun two weeks ago for patients aged 20 and over.

However, the service would accept users aged 18 and over for outpatient clinics.

The program will be launched on February 8 by the Anglican Archbishop of Adelaide, Dr Ian George.

(Marijuananews note: The Archbishop should re-read the 9th Commandment. He is giving false evidence against his neighbors.)
